newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Fiat aims its cars at emerging markets.
newsitem.headline: Fiat aims its cars at emerging markets.

text.p: World car sales growth is shifting to Latin America, Asia and Eastern Europe, and Italian mass car maker Fiat said on Tuesday that it meant to capture these new customers.

Fiat Auto SpA president and chief executive officer Roberto Testore told a conference organised by Automotive News Europe magazine that the company's "178" project was aimed at winning a toehold in emerging new markets.
Once the bridgehead has been established, Fiat would be in a good position to sell its more upmarket products.
Testore said a fundamental shift in world demand for cars is underway.

"Europe, the United States and Japan sold over 28 million units or 75 per cent of the world total in 1995. However the estimates for 2005 suggest that sales will reach 32 million, which means just four million extra in 10 years, which is hardly substantial growth," Testore said in a speech.

"By contrast, the figures for the rest of the world, and by this I mean Latin America, Asia and Eastern Europe, show sales rising from nine million in 1995 to 15 million in 2005, which means a jump from 24 per cent to 32 per cent of the world total," Testore said.
"We believe that the main opportunities in the years ahead lie in these nations whose economies are rapidly expanding," said Testore.
Fiat launched the first of the "178" model cars - the Palio - in Brazil a little over a year ago. Since then 260,000 Palio hatchbacks have been built, in an investment costing $1 billion.

Fiat started making the Palio in Argentina this year, and will also make it in Venezuela. Before the end of 1999, Fiat will make Palio variants in India, and plans production in Turkey, South Africa, and Morocco.

"The 178 will undoubtedly be the biggest volume model in Fiat's history. If all our plans come to fruition we expect to be manufacturing between 900,000 and one million a year by the turn of the century."
"The 178 project wil act as a passport, providing Fiat with an entry to new markets to which we will also be able to export other models," Testore said.

Fiat was the fifth biggest mass car manufacturer in Europe last year with a market share of 11.2 per cent. But so far in 1997 it has made a spectacular rebound, thanks to a government-funded incentive scheme in Italy to persuade people to junk their old fume spewing clunkers.
Fiat's market share in the first four months of 1997 jumped to 12.2 per cent, leapfrogging Ford Motor Co, Peugeot and General Motors Corp into second place behind Germany's Volkswagen AG.

Testore told questioners after his speech that everybody had benfited from this scheme. People were driving more modern, safer, more environmentally friendly cars. Fiat would also be Testore talked extensively about Fiat's globalisation plans. One questioner asked how could Fiat be truly global if it shunned the U.S. market?
"We can be absoluteley global without being there," Testore replied.
